title: In its season
hookLine: figs come in season and go, and so do the people we love
carry: receive the season while it lasts

lines: NOBODY YELLS AT A BARE TREE.
cards: A fig tree, a peach tree, a strawberry patch at a farm stand: for a few weeks each summer the fruit is perfect, and then it's gone. Nobody stands under a bare fig tree in January shouting at it. We know how fruit works.
Epictetus thought we forget it the moment it's a person. In a long talk on not being moved by what isn't ours, book three, chapter twenty-four, he reaches for the fig.

teach.b: To long for a friend or a child when they're no longer given to you, Epictetus says, is like longing for a fig in winter. Not wicked. Just out of season.

The tree was never going to fruit in the snow, and wanting it doesn't change the tree. Then something that makes people wince. When you kiss your child, he says, you might quietly tell yourself: tomorrow you may die.
Someone objects at once: that's an ill-omened thing to say. Is it ill-omened, he asks, to say the grain will be harvested? That leaves fall?
That a fresh fig becomes a dried one, and a grape a raisin? These are only changes, things moving from one state to the next. Nothing in nature is cursed by being named.
The whisper isn't meant to spoil the kiss.

teach.h: NAMING CHANGE IS NOT A CURSE.
teach.b: It makes it real: you kiss a living person who is here now, not a possession you assume you'll always have.
What we love, Epictetus says, is given to us for the present, not forever, like a fig or a bunch of grapes in its season. So the answer isn't to clutch, and it isn't to stop loving.

teach.h: RECEIVE IT, THEN SAY THANK YOU.
teach.b: It's to receive the season while it lasts, and when it ends, one fitting answer is thanks.
Ecclesiastes says it too, in its own way: there is a season for everything. Epictetus says it with a fig.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism remind themselves, gently, that the people they love are with them for a time, and use that reminder to be more present and more grateful rather than more anxious.

o: a sign that a hard winter is coming soon
what we love, given for a season, not forever
a fruit the Stoics ate to stay disciplined

games.q: in its season — tap the pairs.
p: longing for what's out of season

s: in the text, someone calls the kiss advice ill-omened
the objection comes at once, and Epictetus answers with grain, leaves, figs and grapes.
Epictetus says the answer to loss is to stop loving
he says to love what is given while it's given, and to give thanks when it goes.
the fig image comes from Discourses book three
it's in chapter twenty-four, the long talk on things not in our power.

games.q: you're one of Epictetus' students. he's just said to whisper tomorrow you may die while kissing your child. what's your first reaction?
o: that's an ill-omened thing to say.
games.why: in the text, someone says exactly that. he asks back: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested, or that a fig becomes a dried fig?

practice: Bring to mind someone whose season with you has changed, a grandparent, an old friend, someone who moved away or died, and picture one ordinary moment with them: the kitchen, the car, the bench.
Let that season be there for a moment. Then, silently or under your breath, say: thank you for that season.

wordCard.voice: Fig. Epictetus' image for what we love: given for a time, like a fig in its season, so we receive it while it's here and give thanks when it passes.

carryVoice: Your line: receive the season while it lasts. Not clutching, and not loving less. Day four hundred twenty-three, done.
